An SFO provides customised wealth management services tailored to the unique needs and preferences of a single affluent family.
An MFO extends specialised wealth management services to multiple families, sharing expertise and costs among them.
A VFO operates through a tech-driven, flexible structure, often remotely, to manage the wealth of a family or multiple families, making it a cost-effective alternative.

An EFO evolves organically within a successful family business, initially managing the family's wealth alongside the business operations before potentially transitioning to a more formalised structure.
Tailored services to meet the unique needs of a single family.
Cost-effective due to shared expenses among multiple families.
Cost-effective and flexible, especially for families with assets between $10m and $250m
Organic evolution within a family business, offering control, continuity, and support.
Complete control over the family's wealth and assets.
Specialised expertise and investment ideas can be shared among families.
Professionals are already integrated within the business operations.
Emphasis on long-term wealth preservation and growth over short-term profits.
Can offer a range of services, though typically focused on investment management.
Can offer a blend of in-house and outsourced services.
Seamless integration with family business operations
Very high operational costs, often exceeding $1m annually.
Profit-driven, which could potentially shift focus to short-term gains.
Requires sustantial effort from family members to manage, especially as the founding members age.
Potential conflicts of interest among different families served.
Might not suit families desiring a high level of personal interaction of those with complex needs.
May pose tax risks and become cumbersome as the family's financial complexity increases.
Suitable for families with assets between $100m and $400m who desire a high level of control and customisation.
Families with substantial wealth but looking to reduce operational costs and willing to share services with other families.
Families with moderate to high wealth levels seeking a balance between cost effeciency and personalised service, comfortable with a tech-driven approach.
Initially suitable within a successful family business, but may require a transition to another structure as the family's assets and needs grow.
Stock Acquisitions are one of the most common ways companies merge with other entities and is also the technical term for a "hostile takeover."
Vertical Mergers happen when two companies occupy the same industry, but one feeds directly into the other's production line.
A merger between two companies producing different goods & services for one specific finished products.
The merger of the firm that have actual or potential buyer-seller relationship.
E.g. Apple Buys Dr Dre Beats Electronics for $3.2Bn in 2014
Horizontal Mergers work similarly to vertical mergers, but the two companies occupy the same industry and are often competitors.
A merger occurring between companies producing similar products, goods and offerings similar services.
This type of merger occurs frequently as a result of larger companies attempting to create more effective economies of scale.
E.g. Boeing acquired McDonnell Douglas for $13Bn in 1997
Conglomerates form when two companies in separate industries join to diversify their products and spread quickly into other sectors.
Pure conglomerate M&A - It involves firms with nothing common.
Mixed conglomerate merger - It involves firms that are looking for product extensions or market extensions.
E.g. Tata Group acquired Jaguar-Land Rover in 2008 from Ford for $2.3Bn
A Concentric Merger requires two companies in similar, but not identical industries. This kind of alliance is beneficial when the two companies have similar production needs or distribution channels.
An Asset Purchase is used by companies who want specific assets from another company but not their current liabilities or the entirety of the business.

A merger is a result of an agreement between two companies that want to come together and create a new company. This process is normally less complicated compared to the other two. It's why this method is mostly used.
A transaction where two firms agree to integrate their operations on a relatively coequal basis because they have resources and capabilities that together may create a stronger competitive advantage

The buyer buys all the assets of the selling company. This method is considered the best deal structure used to sell a company if the buyer wants to get cash in exchange for the deal. With this, the buyer also chooses the assets that they wish to purchase.
The assets of company Y may be sold to company X. Once this is done company Y is then legally terminated and company X survives.
The selling company will still continue to operate as a corporate entity even after the sale has been made, with its unsold liabilities and assets.
The buyer has the choice to choose the assets they get to buy from the seller and which ones they do not want to purchase.
The deal might take a long time to close as compared to the other M&A deal structure methods.
This process can lead to high-impact tax costs for both parties.
The buyer will not have the choice to acquire any non-transferable assets, such as goodwill.

The stock purchase method does not have the assets transacted directly. The major amount of the voting stock of the seller is acquired by the buyer. This means that the control of the seller’s assets and liabilities is transferred to the buyer.
The common share of company Y may be purchased by company X. When company X holds all the share of company Y, it is dissolve.
It is a less expensive method.
Closing this deal will take less time as it is simpler and requires less negotiations.
The taxes on this deal are low, especially for the seller.
Uncooperative minority shareholders might have an issue with this.
Financial and legal liabilities can come with the stock purchase acquisition.
The company X may give their shares to stakeholders of company Y for its net assets. The company Y terminated by its shareholder who now holds share of company X.
Company X gives its shares to the shareholder of company Y and then company X is terminated.
The financial benefits achieved when 2 companies combine, leading to reduced operating expenses and increased efficiency.
The additional revenue or sales growth generated by accessing new markets, cross-selling products or services, or complementary customer bases to increase sales.
Includes both cost and revenue synergies and may also involve optimising capital structure, improving financial management, and enhancing overall financial health.
The advantages gained by integrating and leveraing the technological assets that lead to improved product development, enhanced R&D capabilities, or faster technological advancements.
Does the target firm strengthen or complement the acquiring firm’s strategy? (N.B. It is easy to over-estimate this potential synergy).
Is there a match between the management practices, cultural practices and staff characteristics of the target and the acquiring firm?
Human Resources (HR): This includes aligning employee benefits, policies, and culture, as well as addressing workforce redundancies.
Finance and Accounting: Integrating financial systems, reporting, and accounting practices to ensure consistency and compliance.
Information Technology (IT): Merging IT infrastructure, systems, and data to enhance efficiency and cybersecurity.
Sales and Marketing: Coordinating sales and marketing strategies, branding, and customer relations to maximize market impact.
Operations and Supply Chain: Optimizing operations, production processes, and supply chain management for cost savings.
Product and Technology: Integrating product offerings and technology platforms for innovation and competitiveness.
Legal and Compliance: Ensuring legal compliance, intellectual property protection, and risk management.
Customer Service and Support: Consolidating customer service and support functions to enhance customer experience.
Real Estate and Facilities: Managing real estate assets, facilities, and office locations for cost—efficiency.
Corporate Culture: Fostering a cohesive corporate culture and addressing cultural differences to promote a harmonious work environment.
Acquirer slowly, over a period of time, buys the shares of the target in the stock market to gain a controlling interest in the company.
A takeover attempt that buys all available shares of the target company at the current market price as soon as the stock exchange is open for business.

The acquirer presents an attractive takeover that the target company cannot refuse. A godfather offer does not have negative implications that are usually associated with this type of takeover offer, including a change of the management team, asset stripping, or transfer of reserves.
Acquirer offers an attractive price to target shareholders to sell their shares in the case of a clean takeover bid.

Purchasing less than 5% of a company’s shares – to obtain a significant equity position, perhaps aiming to eventually gain a controlling interest, but a small enough purchase to avoid having to notify regulatory authorities.
Target selling the most valuable parts of the company (crown jewels) if a hostile takeover occurs. This deters acquirers from pursuing a hostile takeover.

The provision requires that anti-takeover defenses can only be canceled by a vote of the board, so acquirers who want to avoid the consequences of the defenses must receive approval from the board before initiating a takeover.

Target company’s shareholders can purchase more shares of its stock at a discount. This dilutes the stock, making it more expensive and difficult for a potential acquirer to obtain a controlling equity interest (more than 50% of voting shares).
Target company’s shareholders can buy the post-merger (acquirer) company’s stock at a discount. The target company is counterattacking by diluting the acquirer’s stock.
An employment contract that guarantees extensive benefits to executives if they are made to leave the company. This allows executives to remain in the company even after a merger.
Target company repurchasing stock from the acquirer or a third party for a premium price to avoid the stock falling into the hands of the acquirer.
Public relations firms, law firms, or investment bankers hired by a target company to help fend off a hostile takeover.
Restricting individuals with large amounts of convertible securities from converting if by doing so the individual is going to hold 10% or more of the target’s shares.
The target company of a hostile takeover turns around and attempts to obtain controlling shares of the acquirer.
Any of several hostile takeover defenses designed to discourage the acquirer from pursuing the takeover.
Target companies allow bondholders to sell bonds back at a premium to make hostile takeovers costlier.
Target company playing along with the hostile bid and stalling for time while waiting for a white knight to appear.

Target borrows money at extremely high interest rates to make the takeover unattractive. It’s a double-edged sword because although the takeover is prevented, the company may be destroyed by crippling debt.
Target starting litigation to thwart an attempt at a takeover.
A requirement that a very large percentage of shareholders approve of major decisions of the company – an attempt to fend off hostile takeovers.
A friendly takeover bidder that outbids the Black Knight.
An ally of the target company that does not buy enough shares to gain a controlling interest, but enough to prevent the hostile takeover acquirer from gaining a controlling interest.
Extension of scope in terms of geography, products or markets.
Consolidation to increasing scale, efficiency and market power.
Capabilities on enhancing technological know-how (or other competences).
Financial Efficiency for a company with a strong balance sheet (cash rich) may acquire/merge with a company with a weak balance sheet (high debt)
Tax efficiency to reducing the combined tax burden
Asset stripping or unbundling to selling off bits of the acquired company to maximise asset values
Personal ambition on financial incentives tied to short-term growth or share-price targets; boosting personal reputations; giving friends and colleagues greater responsibility or better jobs.
Bandwagon effects where the managers may be branded as conservative if they don’t follow a M&A trend; shareholder pressure to merge or acquire; the company may itself become a takeover target.
Restructuring Strategy is a strategy through which a firm changes its set of businesses or financial structure.
Restructuring Strategy is a strategy through which a firm changes its set of businesses or financial structure.
Restructuring strategy may occur due to changes in the external or internal environments of the firm.
Restructuring now aligned with the aim of increasing shareholder value – a “renewed emphasis upon the maximisation of shareholder wealth”
The sale of unproductive assets, or even whole lines of businesses, that are peripheral.
Changing the debt-equity mix, or the mix between different classes of debt or equity.
Changes in the composition of the top management team, organization structure, and reporting relationships.
A reduction in the number of a firm’s employees and, sometimes, in the number of its operating units.
Expectation of improved profitability from cost reductions.
Desire or necessity for more efficient operations.
Restructuring may or may not change the composition of businesses in the portfolio.
A divestiture, spin-off or some other means of eliminating businesses that are unrelated to a firm’s core businesses.
A set of actions that causes a firm to strategically refocus on its core and related businesses.
Refers to divestiture, spin-off or some other means of eliminating businesses that are unrelated to a firm’s core business.
May be accompanied by downsizing, but not eliminating key employees from its primary businesses.
Following downscoping, the firm can be more effectively managed by the top management team because it has become less diversified.
Significant amounts of debt are usually incurred to finance the buyout.
Often, the intent is to improve efficiency and performance, eventually making the firm an attractive candidate for purchase.
A restructuring strategy whereby a party buys all of a firm’s assets in order to take the firm private
Can correct for managerial mistakes that primarily serve managers’ own interests rather than those of shareholders.
Following LBO, restructuring occurs: downsize and/or downscope.

No one organisation can exist in isolation today. All organisations depend on establishing and developing relationships.

Many commentators predictthat the future of many organisations depend on their ability to successfully enter, and manage, collaborative ventures. The coming decade will be one of strategic collaborations.
Get into critical country markets quickly to accelerate process of building a global presence

Partnerships between firms where their resources, capabilities, and core competencies are combined to pursue mutual interests to develop, manufacture, and distribute goods or services.

Companies sometimes use strategic alliances or collaborative partnerships to complement their own strategic initiatives and strengthen their competitiveness. Such cooperative strategies go beyond normal company-to-company dealings but fall short of merger or full joint venture partnership.
Cooperating with other firms is a strategy that
Exceeds the cost of constructing customer value in other ways.
Establishes a favorable position relative to competition.
Exchange and sharing of resources and capabilities.
Co-development or distribution of goods or services.
It is critical to a company’s achievement of an important objective
It helps build, sustain, or enhance a core competence or competitive advantage
It helps block a competitive threat
It helps open up important market opportunities
It mitigates a significant risk to a company’s business
Equity alliances involve the creation of a new entity that is owned separately by the partners involved.
Non-equity alliances are typically looser, without the commitment implied by ownership.
Production of goods by one firm, under the label or brand of another firm.

Short-term arrangement in which several firms (from the same or different industry sectors or countries) pool their financial and human resources to undertake a large project that benefits all members of the group.
E.g. 6 Singapore firms join hands to team up with international players to vie for high-speed rail contracts (Clifford Capital, DBS, ST Electronics, Surbana Jurong, sembcorp, SMRT)

A joint venture (JV) is a business arrangement in which two or more parties agree to pool their resources for the purpose of accomplishing a specific task. This task can be a new project or any other business activity.
E.g. Golden Harvest JV with Village Roadshow to form Golden Village and Google JV with NASA to form Google Maps
Licensing is where a business arrangement in which one company gives another company permission to manufacture its product for a specified payment.
Franchising is a form of business by which the owner (franchisor) of a product, service or method obtains distribution through affiliated dealers (franchisees).
This is a cooperative strategy wherein a group of firms forms multiple partnerships to achieve shared objectives.
E.g. Oneworld, Star Alliance, Sky Team

The discount rate is the minimum rate of return acceptable to the investor. The absolute value of the discount rate depends on the definition of the discount rate. Namely, for cash flow after debt servicing, a simple discount rate is used, while for cash flow before debt servicing, a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is used.

DCF method can be used in startup valuation when there are reasonable and reliable cash flow projections available. DCF is a popular approach that estimates the present value of a company based on its expected future cash flows. Involves forecasting cash flows and applying discount rate.
Accurate cash flow projects and selection of an appropraite discount rate are crucial.

In startup valuation, traditional metrics like EBITDA multiples aren't primary, given pre-revenue or limited financial data. Instead, focus on methods gauging future growth. EBITDA and market multiples may apply based on financial stability and maturity.

The Comparable Companies Method (Market Comparable or Market Multiple Method) can be used in startup valuation when there are comparable publicly-traded companies or recently funded startups in the same industry. This approach is commonly used in later-stage startups. Uses P/E ratio, P/S ratio and EV/EBITDA.
Ensure you select comparable companies that are truly similar in terms of business model, size and growth prospects.

The Replacement Cost Method or Cost to Duplicate Method is typically not the primary approach in startup valuation. Yet, these methods might be explored if the startup heavily relies on tangible assets with specific characteristics, addressing unique situations in the valuation process.

The Net Book Value (NBV) method is an accounting metric, representing the difference between historical cost and accumulated depreciation on the balance sheet, and is not a prominent factor in determining the value of startups due to its focus on historical accounting values.

The Berkus Method is a rule-of-thumb valuation technique for early-stage startups. Tailored for pre-revenue ventures, it assigns dollar values to qualitative risk factors, acknowledging the limitations of traditional financial metrics in assessing startups without established revenues or earnings.

This method initiates by projecting the startup's future exit value (e.g., [PC or acquisition). The venture capitalist then sets the desired return on investment (ROI), determining the present valuation. It commonly employs multiples and discount rates for present valuations.
CTA looks at recent M&A transactions involving similar companies to estimate the value of the target company.
Be aware of the differences in deal structures and terms between the comparable transactions and your own deal.
Asset-based valuation focuses on the net value of a company's assets, which can include tangible assets (e.g. real estate, equipment) and intangible assets (e.g. patents, trademarks).
Consider the liquidation value (asset sold off) and going concern value (assets used in onging operations).
Asset-Based Valuation = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
Market cap is the total value of a company's outstanding shares of stock. In an acquisition, the acquirer may offer a premium over the target company's market cap.
Market cap is readily available for public companies, making it a straightforward metric.
Market Cap = Share Price x Total Outstanding Shares
Valuation is based on multiples of revenue (e.g. Price-to-Sales ratio) or earnings (e.g. Price-to-Earnings ratio). These multiples are applied to the target company's financial metrics.
Ensure you use appropriate multiples for your industry.
This method assesses the premium (percentage increase) paid by the acquirer over the current market price of the target company's shares.
Evaluate the reasons for the premium, such as strategic value or synergy potential.
Premium Paid = (Offer Price - Market Price) / Market Price
LBO analysis estimates the potential return to an acquiring company if the acquisition is financed through a mix of debt and equity.
Consider the impact of debt financing on the financial structure.
This method calculates the premium an acquirer is willing to pay for control over the target company.
The control premium can vary widely basedo n the circumstances of the acquisition.
Control Premium = (Offer Price for Control - Market Price) / Market Price
This approach focuses on the valuation of intangible assets, such as patents, copyrights, and brand value.
Engage experts if you have valuable intangible assets that need precise valuation.

Represents the mean annual growth rate of an investment over a specified period longer than one year. It is a useful measure to smooth out volatility over multiple periods and provide a single growth rate
A model that describes the relationship between the expected return of an investment and its risk, measured by beta (β)

This approach is based on the idea that the value of a company is directly related to its ability to generate income. This approach is useful for valuing companies that have a predictable income stream and a long-term history of earnings.

This approach assumes that the value of a company is closely related to the prices of comparable companies in the market. The market approach considers the actual market transactions and market data of comparable companies, such as their stock prices, sales, earnings, dividends, and other financial metrics.

This approach is based on the principle that the value of a company is equal to the sum of its assets (equipment, cash, receivables), less the sum of its liabilities (payables, loans). The asset based approach is useful for valuing companies that have significant tangible assets, such as real estate companies.

Crucial for overseeing the entire process, from identifying potential targets or buyers to conducting due diligence and negotiating terms. They provide strategic guidance and ensure the transaction aligns with the startup's objectives
Help the startup smoothly assimilate into the acquiring company or merge with another. They develop integration plans, manage the transistion, and ensure minimal disruption to operations.
Help navigate complex legal issues, contracts and regulatory compliance. They play a critical role in drafting and reviewing agreements and protecting the startup's interests.
Help structure the transaction to minimise tax liabilities, identify potential tax credits, and ensure compliance with tax laws and regulations.
Assist in valuing the startup, negotiating deal terms, and assessing the financial impact of the transaction. They help secure favourable financial terms and ensure a fair valuation.

Financial Statements: Provide detailed financial statements, including income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements.
Tax Records: Furnish tax returns and related documents, including corporate tax returns. sales tax records, and any outstanding or pending tax liabilities.
Legal Documents: Include all legal documents, such as articles of incorporation, bylaws, operating agreements, and any pending or historical litigation records.
Intellectual Property (IP) Documentation: Disclose patents, trademarks, copyrights, and other intellectual property assets owned by the startup.
Customer and Vendor Contracts: Provide copies of key customer and vendor contracts, highlighting any long-term agreements, pricing structures, or contractual obligations.
Employee and HR Records: Share employee contracts, organization charts, compensation plans, and HR-related documents.
Real Estate and Lease Agreements: Include details on owned or leased real estate properties, lease agreements, and any related obligations, such as rent or property maintenance.
Insurance Policies: Provide information on existing insurance policies, including liability, property, and key-person insurance.
Regulatory and Compliance Documents: Share any licenses, permits, or certifications required.
Customer Data and Agreements: If applicable, disclose customer data protection policies, GDPR compliance, and any privacy-related agreements with customers or data providers.

Non-Binding Offer in a M&A Agreement

With an M&A agreement comes a non-binding offer. The non-binding offer, also called the indicative offer, lists all the terms and conditions of a potential buyer in an M&A transaction. It is a simple written offer letter that is signed by authorized staff of those in the deal.

The non-binding offer is not a legally binding one. Therefore, the seller cannot rely on the terms in it. This is used in transactions to get a first glimpse of the way the parties value the business and what terms and conditions they will have in the offer. Only the purchase agreements are the ones that allow the parties to buy and sell. The seller uses the information on the non-binding offer to analyze, compare and review the bids. It is used as a draft to help with the M&A deal.

The agreement sets the rules that the newly acquired company needs to follow until the convergence has been finalized. It also includes the accounting of all the assets and liabilities of both companies and contains the details of how each company’s shares will be valued post the merger.
The merger and acquisition agreement holds many documents that are important to finalize the transfer. One such document is also the share purchase agreement for the mergers and acquisitions process.

An M&A deal structure is a binding agreement that outlines the rights and obligations of both parties. It states what each party gets and what each is obligated to do as per the agreement. Also called the terms and conditions of the merger and acquisition.
The deal structure is prepared by considering the risk weightage of both parties. It needs both parties to state the following things:
How much risk can they take
Observable latent risks and how they can be managed
Conditions under which the negotiations can be canceled
States the terms and conditions of the mergers and acquisitions’ financial investment. These are normally considered to be legally binding unless both parties have stated it.

Outlines the understanding between the parties and their intent in a legally binding agreement. It is not normally considered a legally binding document, except for the binding provisions that have been added to it.

This agreement transfers the individual assets from the seller to the buyer by signing a bill of sale. The first step is to select the acquisition method of how the buyer is purchasing the company. Is it going to be an entity purchase or an asset one? An entity purchase means a majority of the company’s stock, along with the debts and obligations, will go to the new owner. With an asset purchase, the buyer will get all the assets – all the real property like real estate, office equipment, and even intellectual property, including copyrights, trademarks, and patents. The new buyer has the right to start depreciating the new assets instantly as it gives a tax benefit.
